title: Ch 4 — Energy Analysis of Closed Systems
source: Cengel, Boles & Kanoglu — Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 4
description: Boundary work, the closed-system first law, and specific heats.

cards.front: Write the *moving boundary work* for a closed system.
cards.back: $W_b = \displaystyle\int_1^2 P\,dV$ — the area under the process path on a P-V diagram.
$W_b = P_0\,(V_2 - V_1)$, since P is constant and comes out of the integral.

cards.front: Boundary work for *isothermal* expansion of an ideal gas?
cards.back: $W_b = mRT\,\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = P_1 V_1 \ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$ (since PV = const at constant T).
$W_b = \dfrac{P_2 V_2 - P_1 V_1}{1 - n}$ for $n \ne 1$; for $n = 1$ it reduces to $W_b = P_1 V_1 \ln(V_2/V_1)$.

cards.front: State the first law (energy balance) for a closed system.
cards.back: $Q_{net,in} - W_{net,out} = \Delta U + \Delta KE + \Delta PE$. For a stationary closed system: $Q - W = \Delta U = m(u_2 - u_1)$.
$c_v = \left(\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial T}\right)_v$ and $c_p = \left(\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial T}\right)_P$. $c_p > c_v$ because constant-pressure heating also does boundary work.

cards.front: For an ideal gas, what do u and h depend on?
cards.back: Temperature only: $u = u(T)$ and $h = h(T)$. (They do not depend on pressure or specific volume.)

cards.front: Δu and Δh for an ideal gas (average specific heats)?
cards.back: $\Delta u = c_v\,\Delta T$ and $\Delta h = c_p\,\Delta T$.

cards.front: Relation between $c_p$, $c_v$ and R for an ideal gas, and the ratio k?
cards.back: $c_p - c_v = R$ (Mayer's relation), and the specific-heat ratio $k = \dfrac{c_p}{c_v}$.

cards.front: Specific heats and property changes for *incompressible* substances (solids/liquids)?
cards.back: $c_p = c_v = c$. Then $\Delta u = c\,\Delta T$ and $\Delta h = c\,\Delta T + v\,\Delta P$ (the $v\,\Delta P$ term is often negligible).
$W_b = \int P\,dV = 0$ when the volume is constant (a rigid tank).
